title: Local first-order vertex marking in logarithmically many CONGEST rounds
formal: Historical question, resolved positively: for every fixed local first-order graph formula φ(x) and every fixed graph class C of bounded expansion, can a deterministic CONGEST algorithm mark exactly the vertices v satisfying G⊨φ(v) in O(log n) rounds, simultaneously for every n-vertex input graph G∈C? The constructive formulation uses the class’s fixed computable expansion bound.
context:
A formula may depend on only a small-radius neighborhood even when that neighborhood contains many vertices. Collecting the entire neighborhood can overload O(log n)-bit links, so constant logical radius does not automatically yield a fast CONGEST algorithm.

For example, φ(x) can say that x belongs to a triangle. The task is to identify every vertex with that property, not merely to have some node detect that a triangle exists.

Bounded expansion includes planar graphs, bounded-degree graphs and classes excluding a fixed minor. Bounding degeneracy alone is weaker and does not give the same general theorem.

The STOC paper explicitly restates the question cited by the 2024 card and answers it with deterministic O(log n) vertex marking. Its separate theorem for unrestricted FO formulas costs O(D+log n), where D is the diameter; the local target here has no D term.
why: Shows that logical locality can be translated into efficient distributed computation despite narrow communication links throughout a broad family of sparse graph classes.
status_note: Resolved by Blin, Fomin, Fraigniaud, Gay, Golovach, Montealegre, Rapaport and Todinca, STOC 2026. The exact historical question, local formula, bounded-expansion convention, node information and Theorem 4.1’s simultaneous deterministic output were matched. This is published-theorem/model verification, not an independent proof audit or proof-assistant certificate.

definitions: The network is a finite connected undirected simple graph G=(V,E), n=|V|. Nodes have distinct O(log n)-bit identifiers, communication ports and a common polynomial upper bound on n. They communicate synchronously, with O(log n) bits per edge in each direction per round, and unrestricted local computation. No graph decomposition is supplied. A first-order formula uses vertex variables, equality, adjacency, Boolean operations and vertex quantifiers. Here φ has one free variable x. It is local if some fixed radius r makes its truth at v depend only on the rooted induced neighborhood of all vertices at graph distance at most r from v. The formula and r are fixed independently of n. A graph class has bounded expansion if for every integer s≥0 there is a constant b_s bounding the average degree of every s-shallow minor of every graph in the class. Such a minor is formed by contracting pairwise vertex-disjoint connected subgraphs of radius at most s, with optional vertex/edge deletions and with parallel edges and loops suppressed. The constructive source assumes a computable bound as a function of s; the class and its bound are fixed, not arbitrary input. The required output at each node v is a Boolean bit equal to the truth value of φ(v). The hidden round constant may depend on φ and C, but not on n, the graph or the identifiers.
answer_criterion: The affirmative result is Theorem 1.4, formally Theorem 4.1, of the full version published at STOC 2026. It gives exactly the required deterministic simultaneous marking algorithm, and additionally permits a fixed finite set of unary vertex labels.
